Extracting environmental data at observation points

Source: vignettes/articles/extracting-environmental-data-at-points.Rmd
extracting-environmental-data-at-points.Rmd

Marine observations often come with a geographical location, a depth and a date. These may describe an animal location recorded by a tracking device, an observation from a baited remote underwater video system (BRUV), a fishing operation or another type of marine survey. In each case, we may know where and when an observation was recorded but still need to identify its associated environmental conditions.

An environmental dataset rarely contains a measurement at precisely the same coordinates, depth and instant. Instead, it provides values on a grid, at particular depth levels and timestamps. Before assigning a temperature to an observation, we therefore need to decide which of these values represents the observation’s conditions.

What environmental conditions correspond to each fishing observation, and how do our selection rules affect the answer?

In this tutorial, we will use extract_to_point() to answer this question. We will follow one observation through the horizontal, vertical and temporal selections, then extend the workflow to several observations and netCDF files.

Our research question

Imagine we have a small table of fishing records. For each record, we know:

  • Its longitude and latitude, in decimal degrees.
  • Its recorded depth, in metres below the reference surface.
  • Its date and time, with a known time zone.

We would like to add potential temperature at the nearest valid depth, compare this with surface and deeper conditions, and understand where the returned values came from.

The fishing records below are fictional teaching observations. The temperatures are real modelled values from a small Copernicus Marine subset. No external downloads or credentials are needed to run this article.

A point selection describes the recorded location, rather than the full extent of a longline or the path of a trawl. If our question concerns conditions throughout a surrounding volume and time window, the buffer extraction tutorial provides a complementary workflow.

Getting started: preparing our data

The example files accompany this article in the repository’s vignettes/articles/point-data/ directory. To run the code manually, use vignettes/articles/ as your working directory, as when building the article.

library(ocean3d)

# Locate the small real-data subset supplied with this article.
example_dir <- "point-data"
nc_file <- file.path(example_dir, "temperature-points.nc")

# Load the article's display data and plotting helper.
example <- readRDS(file.path(example_dir, "point-display.rds"))
source(file.path(example_dir, "figures.R"))

The plotting helper is specific to this article; it is not an exported ocean3d function. All environmental extractions below use the netCDF files directly.

We begin by creating our observation table. Depths are positive downwards. We use UTC explicitly, preserving the instants recorded in the date column.

observations <- data.frame(
  record = c("set_A", "set_B", "set_C"),
  lon = c(0, 0.08, -0.08),
  lat = c(38, 38.04, 38.06),
  depth = c(60, 100, 200),
  date = as.POSIXct(
    c("2026-09-20 00:00:00", "2026-09-20 00:00:00", "2026-09-21 00:00:00"),
    tz = "UTC"
  )
)

observations
#>   record   lon   lat depth       date
#> 1  set_A  0.00 38.00    60 2026-09-20
#> 2  set_B  0.08 38.04   100 2026-09-20
#> 3  set_C -0.08 38.06   200 2026-09-21

Our example file contains thetao, potential temperature at 50 depth levels, and bottomT, the source product’s temperature-at-the-seafloor variable without a vertical dimension. Both vary with time. An additional artificial cell_id variable is included only to demonstrate static extraction; it is not an environmental measurement.

Step 1: Following one observation into the environmental grid

Let’s focus first on set_A: longitude 0 degrees, latitude 38 degrees, depth 60 m, at midnight UTC on 20 September 2026.

one <- observations[1, ]

Its coordinates identify a point. The environmental values, however, are stored at cell centres and discrete depth levels.

plot_point_context(example)

Figure 1. Following our observation into the dataset. Left: the red cross marks the requested point, the black dot marks the selected cell centre, and the outline identifies the cell containing the observation. Colours show temperature at the layer nearest 60 m on 20 September. Right: the vertical profile at that selected cell and timestamp. The red line marks 60 m and the orange point identifies the nearest valid layer. Lines join the profile points for visual guidance; extraction does not interpolate between them. Coordinates are local distances around 0 degrees E, 38 degrees N.

Step 2: Extracting our first temperature

We can request the valid depth layer closest to our observation with method = "nearest".

nearest <- extract_to_point(
  data = one,
  nc = nc_file,
  var = "thetao",
  method = "nearest",
  output_col = "temperature",
  id_col = "record"
)

nearest
#>   record lon lat depth       date temperature
#> 1  set_A   0  38    60 2026-09-20     15.9467

The original row is retained and a new column contains its selected temperature. output_col lets us choose that column’s name; id_col is checked to exist, so a misspelt identifier column is caught early.

Here, “nearest” refers to depth. Time has its own rule, time_match, and each observation takes the grid cell that contains it.

Step 3: Understanding the horizontal selection

An observation takes the grid cell that contains it. It does not need to coincide with the cell’s centre: in Figure 1, the requested point and the selected centre are a short distance apart, which is a normal selection. set_A lies exactly on the edge between two cells, at 38 degrees N, so it takes the cell south of the edge, as any point on an edge between two cells takes the cell east or south of it.

The supplied subset is intentionally small. A point just outside its coverage gets NA, even when it is close to a cell in the subset:

outside <- one
outside$lon <- example$locations$lon[2]

extract_to_point(outside, nc_file, var = "thetao", method = "nearest")
#>   record       lon lat depth       date thetao
#> 1  set_A 0.2175002  38    60 2026-09-20     NA

extract_to_point() doesn’t search for a nearby cell. For a point just outside the grid or in a cell without data, such as near the coast, decide on its location first, or summarise the values around it with the buffer extraction tutorial.

Step 4: Choosing a depth selection

Different research questions call for different parts of the water column. You choose the depth level with method:

method Selection
"nearest" Layer with a value closest to the requested depth; at a tie, the shallower layer.
"surface" Physically shallowest layer, even if its value is missing.
"bottom" Deepest layer with a value in that cell’s profile.
"2d" (default) Variable without a depth dimension, or with one depth layer.

Let’s obtain our nearest, surface and bottom temperatures.

depth_methods <- c(nearest = "nearest", surface = "surface",
                   deepest_valid = "bottom")
sapply(depth_methods, function(m) {
  extract_to_point(one, nc_file, var = "thetao", method = m)$thetao
})
#>       nearest       surface deepest_valid 
#>      15.94670      26.52825      13.79936

Surface and bottom selection do not require an observation depth column. They are defined by the physical depth coordinates and valid values in the profile, rather than the order in which layers were stored. When var is left out and detected, the columns are named nearest_<var>, surface_<var> and seabottom_<var>. Despite its name, seabottom_<var> is the deepest layer with a value, which may be above the real seabed.

Nearest selection is not interpolation, and it does not impose a maximum vertical distance. A request beyond the available depth range can return a distant valid layer; decide whether that selection is appropriate for the analysis.

Our subset retains all 50 original depth levels, down to approximately 398.54 m. The deepest valid thetao value is therefore the deepest value available in that profile, not necessarily a measurement at the seabed.

4.1. Reading a variable without a depth dimension

The source also provides bottomT, a separate temperature-at-the-seafloor variable. We use method = "2d", the default, because that variable has no vertical axis. It still has a time axis and therefore still requires a date.

deepest_valid <- extract_to_point(one, nc_file, var = "thetao",
                                  method = "bottom")$thetao
provider_bottom <- extract_to_point(
  data = one,
  nc = nc_file,
  var = "bottomT",
  output_col = "provider_bottom_temperature"
)

data.frame(
  deepest_valid_thetao = deepest_valid,
  provider_bottom_temperature = provider_bottom$provider_bottom_temperature
)
#>   deepest_valid_thetao provider_bottom_temperature
#> 1             13.79936                    13.20377

These columns need not be equal: one selects a layer from the supplied thetao profile; the other reads the provider’s separate bottomT variable.

Step 5: Matching observations to timestamps

Our first observation coincided with a dataset timestamp. In practice, observations often fall between records. Let’s move it to midday.

midday <- one
midday$date <- as.POSIXct("2026-09-20 12:00:00", tz = "UTC")

extract_to_point(midday, nc_file, var = "thetao", method = "nearest",
                 time_match = "nearest")
#>   record lon lat depth                date  thetao
#> 1  set_A   0  38    60 2026-09-20 12:00:00 15.9467

With time_match = "nearest" (the default), each observation takes the closest time step; with "exact", it needs a step at the same time. A date-time such as this one is compared as an instant, and a Date by its UTC day. The nearest rule sets no maximum time gap on its own.

5.1. Limiting the accepted time gap

max_time_diff is in days, even for date-times. For example, 0.1 days is 2.4 hours, so neither neighbouring midnight satisfies this limit for our midday observation.

extract_to_point(midday, nc_file, var = "thetao", method = "nearest",
                 max_time_diff = 0.1)
#>   record lon lat depth                date thetao
#> 1  set_A   0  38    60 2026-09-20 12:00:00     NA

The result is NA. To require a step on the same UTC day instead of the same instant, give the date without the hour and match exactly:

same_day <- midday
same_day$date <- as.Date("2026-09-20")
extract_to_point(same_day, nc_file, var = "thetao", method = "nearest",
                 time_match = "exact")
#>   record lon lat depth       date  thetao
#> 1  set_A   0  38    60 2026-09-20 15.9467

This reads a record labelled on that day; it does not calculate a daily average.

5.2. Preserving hours and time zones

A Date or date-only ISO string compares by UTC day. A POSIXct/POSIXlt object or ISO date-time keeps the hour and compares the instant. This follows the observation’s precision, not the file’s sampling frequency.

Let’s represent the original midnight UTC observation in Madrid time.

local_time <- one
local_time$date <- as.POSIXct("2026-09-20 02:00:00", tz = "Europe/Madrid")

utc_result <- extract_to_point(one, nc_file, var = "thetao",
                               method = "nearest", time_match = "exact")
local_result <- extract_to_point(local_time, nc_file, var = "thetao",
                                 method = "nearest", time_match = "exact")

data.frame(utc = utc_result$thetao, madrid = local_result$thetao)
#>       utc  madrid
#> 1 15.9467 15.9467

These represent the same instant and return the same value. Calendar days are compared in UTC, so a local date can correspond to the previous UTC day.

For text, use unambiguous ISO dates such as "2026-09-20", or date-times such as "2026-09-20T00:00:00Z". Date-time text is read as UTC, with or without the Z, so text recorded in local time gives the wrong instant. Numeric offsets and zone names in text are not accepted; construct a POSIXct object with the intended zone instead. Resolve ambiguous daylight-saving times when creating that object.

unspecified_zone <- one
unspecified_zone$date <- "2026-09-20 00:00:00"

# Read as midnight UTC.
extract_to_point(unspecified_zone, nc_file, var = "thetao", method = "nearest")
#>   record lon lat depth                date  thetao
#> 1  set_A   0  38    60 2026-09-20 00:00:00 15.9467

Step 6: Extending the workflow to tables, variables and files

We can now apply the same rules to every observation in our table.

environment <- extract_to_point(
  data = observations,
  nc = nc_file,
  var = "thetao",
  method = "nearest",
  output_col = "temperature",
  id_col = "record"
)

environment
#>   record   lon   lat depth       date temperature
#> 1  set_A  0.00 38.00    60 2026-09-20    15.94670
#> 2  set_B  0.08 38.04   100 2026-09-20    15.01775
#> 3  set_C -0.08 38.06   200 2026-09-21    13.88106

Rows and their order are retained. extract_to_point() reads each time step once for all the observations at that time, so a large table needs few reads. var takes one variable, so to add another, call again with the previous result as the input table.

environment <- extract_to_point(
  data = environment,
  nc = nc_file,
  var = "bottomT",
  output_col = "bottom_temperature"
)

environment[, c("record", "temperature", "bottom_temperature")]
#>   record temperature bottom_temperature
#> 1  set_A    15.94670           13.20377
#> 2  set_B    15.01775           13.19387
#> 3  set_C    13.88106           13.61041

Choose distinct output names for different quantities: a column that already exists is an error rather than being overwritten. output_col is the preferred naming option and overrides the older output_prefix.

6.1. A static variable does not need a date

The cell_id layer is an artificial static identifier included for this teaching example. It has no time or depth dimension, even though the same file also contains temporal, three-dimensional temperatures.

locations <- observations[, c("record", "lon", "lat")]

extract_to_point(locations, nc_file, var = "cell_id", output_col = "grid_cell")
#>   record   lon   lat grid_cell
#> 1  set_A  0.00 38.00        32
#> 2  set_B  0.08 38.04        43
#> 3  set_C -0.08 38.06        48

The need for a date follows the selected variable, not the presence of a time dimension elsewhere in the file.

6.2. A series of files, one per date

The example also includes two files containing only thetao, one for 19 September and another for 21 September, on the same grid. Several files of one variable on one grid are read as a series: their time steps are put in time order and joined, so the order we list them in doesn’t matter.

files <- file.path(example_dir, c(
  "temperature-2026-09-19.nc",
  "temperature-2026-09-21.nc"
))

later <- observations[3, ]
first_order <- extract_to_point(later, files, var = "thetao",
                                method = "nearest", output_col = "temperature")
reverse_order <- extract_to_point(later, rev(files), var = "thetao",
                                  method = "nearest",
                                  output_col = "temperature")

data.frame(first_order = first_order$temperature,
           reverse_order = reverse_order$temperature)
#>   first_order reverse_order
#> 1    13.88106      13.88106

Both return the 21 September value. Files on different grids, such as spatial tiles, are not one series: call extract_to_point() once per grid.

These daily files each contain a single data variable, so automatic variable detection is possible when var is omitted. The main example file contains several variables and needs an explicit choice.

extract_to_point(later, files, method = "nearest", output_col = "temperature")
#>   record   lon   lat depth       date temperature
#> 3  set_C -0.08 38.06   200 2026-09-21    13.88106

Step 7: Distinguishing missing observations from invalid requests

An explicit missing date is different from a missing column or an invalid date string. Let’s keep both a valid row and a row whose date is NA.

with_missing <- observations[1:2, ]
with_missing$date[2] <- NA

extract_to_point(with_missing, nc_file, var = "thetao", method = "nearest",
                 id_col = "record")
#> Warning: 1 of 2 points has no time, but variable `thetao` has 3 time steps, so
#> their values are NA. Give the points a time in as_vector3d().
#>   record  lon   lat depth       date  thetao
#> 1  set_A 0.00 38.00    60 2026-09-20 15.9467
#> 2  set_B 0.08 38.04   100       <NA>      NA

Both rows remain in the output, but the second temperature is NA, with a warning that says how many observations had no time. A static-variable extraction can still succeed for that same row. Similarly, a missing requested depth leaves the nearest-depth value missing, while surface and bottom values, which need no depth, are still available.

missing_depth <- one
missing_depth$depth <- NA_real_

sapply(c(nearest = "nearest", surface = "surface", bottom = "bottom"),
       function(m) {
         extract_to_point(missing_depth, nc_file, var = "thetao",
                          method = m)$thetao
       })
#>  nearest  surface   bottom 
#>       NA 26.52825 13.79936

If the date column is absent for a temporal variable, the request is invalid:

without_date <- one[, setdiff(names(one), "date")]
extract_to_point(without_date, nc_file, var = "thetao", method = "nearest")
#> Error:
#> ! `data` has no column date.

A date written in an ambiguous format is invalid as well:

invalid_date <- one
invalid_date$date <- "20/09/2026"
extract_to_point(invalid_date, nc_file, var = "thetao", method = "nearest")
#> Error:
#> ! Time values could not be converted. Invalid date/time.
#> Input: column `date`
#> Affected observations: 1.
#> row/position 1: "20/09/2026"
#> Use Date, POSIXct/POSIXlt, YYYY-MM-DD, YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM or YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.
#> Text timestamps are interpreted in UTC. For another time zone, supply a POSIXct/POSIXlt object.

The message names the affected input and original value, and lists the accepted formats. A date that was NA to begin with is not an error.

These errors are intentionally printed in this tutorial. They show requests that need correction, rather than conditions to solve by silently widening the time tolerance.

For other datasets, also inspect the coordinate metadata. Depths stored in supported metre, centimetre or kilometre units are converted to physical metres, with their positive direction taken into account. Pressure, sigma and formula-based vertical coordinates need an explicit conversion rather than being treated as metre depths. Nonstandard time calendars likewise need compatible handling; see as_proxy() for supported cases.

Step 8 (extra): Adapting the input to our own workflow

8.1. Custom observation-column names 

custom <- one
names(custom) <- c("operation", "longitude", "latitude", "fishing_depth", "when")

extract_to_point(
  custom, nc_file, var = "thetao", method = "nearest",
  lon_col = "longitude", lat_col = "latitude", depth_col = "fishing_depth",
  date_col = "when", id_col = "operation", output_col = "temperature"
)
#>   operation longitude latitude fishing_depth       when temperature
#> 1     set_A         0       38            60 2026-09-20     15.9467

For nonstandard netCDF dimension names, lon_dim, lat_dim, depth_dim and time_dim provide explicit overrides. These refer to file dimensions, whereas the *_col arguments refer to observation columns.

8.2. Direct coordinates and scalar recycling

extract_to_point() can also receive coordinate vectors without an observation table, and returns one value per point. A scalar depth or date is recycled across points.

extract_to_point(
  nc = nc_file, var = "thetao", method = "nearest",
  lon = c(0, 0.08), lat = c(38, 38.04), depth = 60,
  date = as.POSIXct("2026-09-20", tz = "UTC")
)
#> [1] 15.94670 15.98264

8.3. Spatial objects

An sf input retains its POINT geometry:

spatial_observations <- sf::st_as_sf(observations, coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)
extract_to_point(spatial_observations, nc_file, var = "thetao", method = "nearest")
#> Simple feature collection with 3 features and 4 fields
#> Geometry type: POINT
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: -0.08 ymin: 38 xmax: 0.08 ymax: 38.06
#> Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84
#>   record depth       date            geometry   thetao
#> 1  set_A    60 2026-09-20        POINT (0 38) 15.94670
#> 2  set_B   100 2026-09-20  POINT (0.08 38.04) 15.01775
#> 3  set_C   200 2026-09-21 POINT (-0.08 38.06) 13.88106

Data frames, matrices with column names and named lists are also supported. If using a matrix, remember that combining different types can convert columns to text; longitude and latitude must remain numeric at extraction.

8.4. A connection owned by the caller

An already opened ncdf4 connection remains usable after extraction. The caller is responsible for closing it.

local({
  connection <- ncdf4::nc_open(nc_file)
  on.exit(ncdf4::nc_close(connection))

  result <- extract_to_point(one, connection, var = "thetao", method = "nearest")
  print(ncdf4::ncatt_get(connection, "thetao", "units"))
  result
})
#> $hasatt
#> [1] TRUE
#> 
#> $value
#> [1] "degrees_C"
#>   record lon lat depth       date  thetao
#> 1  set_A   0  38    60 2026-09-20 15.9467

Summary

We have assigned environmental values to fishing observations and traced how each request selects a cell, depth layer and timestamp. Along the way, we have:

  1. Used extract_to_point() with each of its four depth methods.
  2. Seen that an observation takes the cell that contains it, and gets NA off the grid.
  3. Compared nearest, surface and bottom layers without interpolation.
  4. Preserved observation hours and time zones, and applied explicit temporal limits.
  5. Read a series of files, named outputs and distinguished missing values from invalid inputs.

The complete basic workflow remains short:

result <- extract_to_point(
  data = observations,
  nc = nc_file,
  var = "thetao",
  method = "nearest",
  time_match = "nearest",
  max_time_diff = 1,
  output_col = "temperature",
  id_col = "record"
)

The one-day time limit is an example choice, not a universal recommendation. Choose settings that match the meaning and precision of your observations.

extract_to_point() is a short wrapper over the package’s build and intersect steps: as_vector3d() builds the points, as_proxy() describes the file and extract() reads the value at every point. The workflow article shows those steps directly, and how to summarise values in buffers, areas and along tracks.

Next steps

  • See extract_to_point() for supported inputs and detailed selection rules.
  • Explore the buffer tutorial when the question concerns a surrounding space and time window.
  • Return to Getting started with ocean3d to explore species’ three-dimensional distributions.

Data sources and reproducibility

The temperature subset comes from Mediterranean Sea Physics Reanalysis, product MEDSEA_MULTIYEAR_PHY_006_004, dataset cmems_mod_med_phy-temp_my_4.2km_P1D-m_202511, downloaded on 19 October 2026. The original temperature values and all 50 downloaded depth levels are retained, with a small spatial crop and three selected dates. The two daily files contain subsets of those same original values. The fishing records and static cell_id field are explicitly artificial teaching data.

E.U. Copernicus Marine Service Information; https://doi.org/10.48670/mds-00375. Source temperatures remain subject to the Copernicus Marine Service licence. The tutorial does not imply endorsement by Copernicus Marine or CMCC.

The repository’s data-raw/point-article.R recreates the files and Figure 1’s display data.

All arguments and defaults

Expand or collapse the complete extract_to_point() signature

This signature is generated from the current function. Arguments without a default require input. A vector lists alternatives with the default first; choose one alternative when calling the function.

extract_to_point(
  # Data and sources
  data = NULL, nc, var = NULL,

  # Direct observation coordinates
  lon = NULL, lat = NULL, depth = NULL, date = NULL,

  # Depth selection
  method = c("2d", "surface", "bottom", "nearest"),

  # Observation and output columns
  lon_col = "lon", lat_col = "lat", depth_col = "depth", date_col = "date",
  output_col = NULL, output_prefix = NULL, id_col = NULL,

  # Source dimensions
  lon_dim = NULL, lat_dim = NULL, depth_dim = NULL, time_dim = NULL,

  # Temporal selection
  time_match = c("nearest", "exact"), max_time_diff = NULL
)
Decision Choices, meaning and effective default
Input and variable data = NULL uses direct lon/lat/depth/date inputs; supply a table, matrix, named list or sf points instead. Dates are required only for variables with several time steps. nc is a file path, several paths of a series on one grid, or an open connection; var = NULL detects a single data variable.
method "2d" (default) for a variable without depth or with one depth layer; "nearest" takes the layer with a value closest to the requested depth; "surface" takes the physically shallowest layer; "bottom" takes the deepest layer with a value.
Horizontal cell Each observation takes the cell that contains it; an observation off the grid gets NA.
time_match "nearest" (default) chooses the nearest time step; "exact" requires a step at the same instant (date-time) or on the same UTC day (date). max_time_diff = NULL has no time-distance limit; a nonnegative value limits it in days.
Missing dates A static variable needs no date. A temporal variable requires the date input or column. An explicit NA keeps the row and returns a missing value, with a warning.
Input names lon_col, lat_col, depth_col, date_col default to lon, lat, depth, date. id_col = NULL means no identifier column; a given one is checked to exist. Dimension names default to NULL (detect); set lon_dim, lat_dim, depth_dim or time_dim to override.
Output name output_col = NULL uses the variable name, or nearest_, surface_ or seabottom_ with it when var is detected; output_prefix is the older name for the same choice. A column that already exists is an error.

See extract_to_point() for accepted formats, units and the full output description.
